tagline: Ancient highlands where coffee was born
overview:
Ethiopia rises from the Horn of Africa as a great mountain plateau, so high and cool that its capital, Addis Ababa, at 2,355 meters, is one of the highest capital cities in the world. The country is about twice the size of Texas and is landlocked, bordered by Eritrea, Djibouti, Somalia, Kenya, South Sudan, and Sudan. With about 125 million people, it is the second most populous country in Africa after Nigeria, and one of the fastest-growing economies on the continent.

Amharic is the official working language, written in its own curvy script called fidel, but more than 80 languages are spoken, including Oromo, Somali, and Tigrinya. Ethiopia is unusual in Africa because it was never colonized, apart from a five-year Italian occupation, and its Orthodox Christian church, ancient calendar, and traditions go back nearly 2,000 years. Today it is a federal republic divided into regions based on ethnic groups. Most Ethiopians farm, growing teff, coffee, and grains, and the country is the birthplace of coffee itself.
landAndNature: The Ethiopian Highlands, sometimes called the Roof of Africa, cover most of the country and are split by the Great Rift Valley, a giant crack in the Earth dotted with lakes. In the Simien Mountains, peaks over 4,500 meters drop in sheer cliffs, and gelada monkeys graze the grassy plateaus while walia ibex cling to the rocks. The Bale Mountains are home to the Ethiopian wolf, the rarest wild dog in the world. To the northeast the land plunges into the Danakil Depression, one of the hottest places on Earth, where the Erta Ale volcano keeps a permanent lava lake. The Blue Nile begins at Lake Tana and thunders over the Blue Nile Falls. Ethiopia has more unique species than almost any other African country, including the lammergeier vulture and the mountain nyala antelope.
peopleAndCulture: Ethiopians eat from a shared platter of injera, a spongy sourdough flatbread made from tiny teff grains, tearing pieces to scoop up spicy stews called wat; doro wat, chicken stew with a hard-boiled egg, is the festive favorite. Coffee is served in a ceremony where beans are roasted, ground, and brewed three times while incense burns. Ethiopia follows its own calendar, about seven years behind the Western one, with 13 months, and celebrates Timket, the Epiphany festival, with processions of priests under embroidered umbrellas. Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity and Islam are both centuries old here. The country is famous for distance runners such as Abebe Bikila, Haile Gebrselassie, and Tirunesh Dibaba, and its music uses a distinctive five-note scale.
history: Some of the oldest human ancestor fossils, including the 3.2-million-year-old Lucy, were found in Ethiopia. The Kingdom of Aksum, from about 100 to 900, was a trading power that raised giant stone obelisks and adopted Christianity around 330. In the 1100s and 1200s the churches of Lalibela were carved straight down into solid rock. Emperors ruled for centuries, and in 1896 Emperor Menelik II defeated an invading Italian army at Adwa, keeping Ethiopia independent when nearly all of Africa was colonized. Italy occupied the country from 1936 to 1941. Emperor Haile Selassie was overthrown in 1974 by a Marxist military junta, whose rule brought war and a terrible famine in 1984 and 1985. Rebels took power in 1991, and Eritrea split away in 1993. A civil war in the Tigray region from 2020 to 2022 killed many thousands.
funFacts: Legend says a goat herder named Kaldi discovered coffee in Ethiopia after noticing his goats dancing from eating red berries.
Ethiopia's calendar has 13 months, twelve of 30 days and one of five or six, and the year 2016 began in September 2023.
The churches of Lalibela were carved downward out of solid rock, so their roofs are level with the ground.
The fossil skeleton called Lucy, found in Ethiopia in 1974, belonged to a human ancestor who lived 3.2 million years ago.
Abebe Bikila won the 1960 Olympic marathon in Rome running barefoot, then won again in 1964 wearing shoes.
